`inla_vanilla()` knows nothing about levels or clusters: it sees one
log-posterior and a vector of parameters. A multilevel model fits in that
mould when the random effects are integrated out inside `logpost`, so that
the parameters are only the fixed effects and the variance components. For a
linear mixed model the integral is in closed form.

This article fits a model with correlated random intercepts and slopes, draws
the random effects from the fit afterwards, and compares both with
[brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) (Bürkner, 2017), which samples the full
model, random effects included, with Stan.

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(inlavanilla)
data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")
```

## The model

The `sleepstudy` data (Belenky et al., 2003; Bates et al., 2015) record the
reaction times $y_{ij}$ of 18 subjects over 10 days of sleep deprivation. Each
subject $j$ has their own intercept and slope:

$$
y_{ij} = \beta_0 + u_{0j} + (\beta_1 + u_{1j})\,\text{day}_{ij} +
\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} u_{0j} \\ u_{1j} \end{pmatrix} \sim N(0, G),
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$

where $G$ has standard deviations $\tau_0$ and $\tau_1$ and correlation
$\rho$. Integrating out $u_j$ leaves, for each subject's vector of reaction
times,

$$
y_j \sim N\left(X_j \beta,\; X_j G X_j^\top + \sigma^2 I\right),
$$

with $X_j = [1, \text{day}_j]$. The priors are $\beta_0, \beta_1 \sim N(0,
500^2)$, half-normal $N(0, 50^2)$ on $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$ and $\sigma$, and a
uniform prior on $\rho$.

## The log-posterior

The standard deviations are on the log scale and $\rho$ on the atanh scale,
so each prior gets the log-Jacobian of its transform: $\log \tau$ for a
standard deviation, and $\log(1 - \rho^2)$ for the correlation.

```{r}
#| label: logpost
logpost <- function(theta, ys, xs) {
  b <- c(theta[["b0"]], theta[["b1"]])
  tau <- exp(c(theta[["log_tau0"]], theta[["log_tau1"]]))
  rho <- tanh(theta[["atanh_rho"]])
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  g <- diag(tau^2)
  g[1, 2] <- g[2, 1] <- rho * tau[1] * tau[2]

  # Marginal log-likelihood, one subject at a time
  loglik <- 0
  for (j in seq_along(ys)) {
    x <- xs[[j]]
    r <- chol(x %*% g %*% t(x) + diag(sigma^2, nrow(x)))
    z <- backsolve(r, ys[[j]] - x %*% b, transpose = TRUE)
    loglik <- loglik - sum(log(diag(r))) - sum(z^2) / 2 -
      nrow(x) / 2 * log(2 * pi)
  }

  # Half-normal prior on a standard deviation, with the log-Jacobian
  lp_sd <- function(s) dnorm(s, 0, 50, log = TRUE) + log(2) + log(s)
  loglik +
    sum(dnorm(b, 0, 500, log = TRUE)) +
    sum(lp_sd(tau)) +
    lp_sd(sigma) +
    log(1 / 2) + log(1 - rho^2)
}
```

The data go in as one response vector and one design matrix per subject:

```{r}
#| label: data
by_subject <- split(sleepstudy, sleepstudy$Subject)
ys <- lapply(by_subject, function(d) d$Reaction)
xs <- lapply(by_subject, function(d) cbind(1, d$Days))
```

## The fit

```{r}
#| label: fit
init <- c(
  b0 = 250, b1 = 10, log_tau0 = log(20), log_tau1 = log(5),
  atanh_rho = 0, log_sigma = log(25)
)
fit <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init, ys = ys, xs = xs)
fit
```

The marginals are on the unconstrained scale. Draws give the standard
deviations and the correlation on their natural scale:

```{r}
#| label: natural
natural <- function(theta) {
  c(
    b0 = theta[["b0"]],
    b1 = theta[["b1"]],
    tau0 = exp(theta[["log_tau0"]]),
    tau1 = exp(theta[["log_tau1"]]),
    rho = tanh(theta[["atanh_rho"]]),
    sigma = exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  )
}
set.seed(1)
draws <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 20000, fun = natural)
```

## Checking against brms

The same model in brms, with the same priors:

```{r}
#| label: brms
#| eval: false
library(brms)
fit_brms <- brm(
  Reaction ~ 0 + Intercept + Days + (Days | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy,
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(0, 500), class = b),
    prior(normal(0, 50), class = sd),
    prior(normal(0, 50), class = sigma),
    prior(lkj(1), class = cor)
  ),
  chains = 4, iter = 7500, warmup = 2500,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.999)
)
```

Its 20,000 draws, with no divergent transitions, were summarised ahead of time
(`lab/multilevel-article.R` in the package source), so this page does not need
Stan to build:

```{r}
#| label: reference
ref <- readRDS("multilevel-brms.rds")

compare <- function(draws, ref) {
  data.frame(
    brms_mean = ref$summary$mean,
    vanilla_mean = colMeans(draws),
    brms_sd = ref$summary$sd,
    vanilla_sd = apply(draws, 2, sd)
  )
}
round(compare(draws, ref$subjects_18), 3)
```

The means agree to a small fraction of a standard deviation. The variance
components and $\rho$ have about the right spread too. The fixed effects are
about 10% too narrow, for a reason the last section explains. The densities,
brms in grey:

```{r}
#| label: densities
plot_compare <- function(draws, ref) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in colnames(draws)) {
    d_ref <- ref$density[[p]]
    d_iv <- density(draws[, p], n = 256)
    plot(
      d_ref$x, d_ref$y, type = "l", lwd = 4, col = "grey75",
      ylim = c(0, max(d_ref$y, d_iv$y)), xlab = p, ylab = "", yaxt = "n"
    )
    lines(d_iv, lwd = 1.5, col = "#B5772E")
  }
}
plot_compare(draws, ref$subjects_18)
```

`inla_vanilla()` took a fraction of a second. brms takes seconds to sample,
after about a minute compiling the model.

## The random effects

The fit has no random effects, because `logpost` integrated them out, but
draws bring them back. Given the parameters $\theta$, each subject's random
effects are Gaussian:

$$
u_j \mid y, \theta \sim N(m_j, V_j),
\qquad
V_j = \left(G^{-1} + X_j^\top X_j / \sigma^2\right)^{-1},
\qquad
m_j = V_j X_j^\top (y_j - X_j \beta) / \sigma^2.
$$

So a draw of $\theta$ from the fit, followed by a draw of each $u_j$ given
$\theta$, is a draw from the posterior of the random effects. `sampling()`
passes `ys` and `xs` on to `fun`:

```{r}
#| label: ranef
draw_ranef <- function(theta, ys, xs) {
  b <- c(theta[["b0"]], theta[["b1"]])
  tau <- exp(c(theta[["log_tau0"]], theta[["log_tau1"]]))
  rho <- tanh(theta[["atanh_rho"]])
  sigma <- exp(theta[["log_sigma"]])
  g <- diag(tau^2)
  g[1, 2] <- g[2, 1] <- rho * tau[1] * tau[2]
  g_inv <- solve(g)

  # One draw of (u0, u1) for each subject, given theta
  u <- vapply(
    names(ys),
    function(j) {
      x <- xs[[j]]
      v <- solve(g_inv + crossprod(x) / sigma^2)
      m <- v %*% crossprod(x, ys[[j]] - x %*% b) / sigma^2
      drop(m + t(chol(v)) %*% rnorm(2))
    },
    numeric(2)
  )
  c(u0 = u[1, ], u1 = u[2, ])
}
set.seed(1)
u_draws <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 20000, fun = draw_ranef, ys = ys, xs = xs)
```

A caterpillar plot shows each subject's posterior mean and 95% credible
interval, sorted by the mean, with brms in grey:

```{r}
#| label: caterpillar
#| fig.height: 5
plot_caterpillar <- function(u_draws, ref) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 3.5, 1, 1))
  on.exit(par(op))
  xlabs <- c(u0 = "Intercept, u0 (ms)", u1 = "Slope, u1 (ms per day)")
  for (k in names(xlabs)) {
    d <- u_draws[, startsWith(colnames(u_draws), k)]
    est <- cbind(colMeans(d), t(apply(d, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))))
    est_ref <- as.matrix(ref$ranef[[k]][, c("mean", "2.5%", "97.5%")])
    o <- order(est[, 1])
    y <- seq_along(o)
    plot(
      est[o, 1], y, type = "n", xlim = range(est, est_ref),
      xlab = xlabs[[k]], ylab = "", yaxt = "n"
    )
    axis(2, at = y, labels = rownames(est_ref)[o], las = 1, cex.axis = 0.7)
    abline(v = 0, col = "grey85")
    segments(est_ref[o, 2], y, est_ref[o, 3], y, lwd = 4, col = "grey75")
    segments(est[o, 2], y, est[o, 3], y, lwd = 1.5, col = "#B5772E")
    points(est[o, 1], y, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = "#B5772E")
  }
}
plot_caterpillar(u_draws, ref$subjects_18)
```

The means agree with brms to within 1% of the interval's width, and the
intervals are at most 5% narrower.

## With fewer subjects

With only the first six subjects, the variance components are poorly
determined:

```{r}
#| label: fit-6
keep <- 1:6
fit_6 <- inla_vanilla(logpost, init, ys = ys[keep], xs = xs[keep])
set.seed(1)
draws_6 <- sampling(fit_6, nsamp = 20000, fun = natural)
round(compare(draws_6, ref$subjects_6), 3)
```

The variance components still match, but the fixed effects are now well too
narrow: the standard deviation of $\beta_1$ is a third too small. Given the
variance components, $\beta$ is Gaussian, but its marginal mixes those
Gaussians over the uncertain $\tau_0$, $\tau_1$ and $\rho$, which gives it
heavier tails than a skew-normal has. `summary()` flags this as a large ridge
bend:

```{r}
#| label: summary-6
summary(fit_6)
```

```{r}
#| label: densities-6
plot_compare(draws_6, ref$subjects_6)
```

The approximation holds up well when the data identify the variance
components, and says so when they do not.
